docs.title: Sapling SAS macros
docs.text:
SAS macros for the tables, listings and figures of clinical trials. A program that uses them reads like the table it makes. Every number the table prints is also written, with its full value, to a numbers file that a second program can check.

Proven against pharmaverse

On six published outputs of the R Consortium R Submission Pilot 1 and the pharmaverse examples, 2,181 of 2,196 numbers are the same in SAS. 14 more differ for a known reason that the check reproduces from the SAS numbers; 1 is a statistic no macro computes. What the proof shows

A table of age and sex by treatment, from the example data:

%describe(data=adsl, var=age, by=trt01a, total=yes, label="Age (years)", out=t_age)
%freq(data=adsl, var=sex, by=trt01a, total=yes, label="Sex", out=t_sex)
%stack(t_age t_sex, out=t14_2_01)

TITLE1 "Table 14-2.01 Age and sex";
%table(
     data  = t14_2_01
   , n     = adsl
   , var   = trt01a
   , order = trt01an
   , total = yes
   , file  = &spl_out./tlf/t14_2_01
 )

tlf/t14_2_01.lst: 15 lines

docs.title: Where to go
docs.text:
• Tutorial: make your first table from the example data, step by step.
  • How-to guides: make a demographic table, an adverse event table, a model table, a figure.
  • Reference: every macro, its parameters, its result, an example and its output.
  • Explanation: how a program reads, the result shape, the numbers, the proof.

docs.title: License
docs.text:
The macros are source available, not open source: the code and the proof are public to read. The terms of use are in the LICENSE of the repository.

To use the macros for a commercial purpose, and for the price, write to DataStep Labs: datastep.studio@gmail.com.

This manual describes the library version 1.10.0.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The words the manual uses with one fixed meaning.

block The rows of a table that one call of a statistics macro makes, under one label (label=). A table is a stack of blocks. columns data set The data set %columns makes: one row per column of the table, with its value, its N and its header. display data set The data set %layout makes: one row per printed line of the table, ROW for the label and C1, C2, ... for the cells. %print prints it. example data The data sets in examples/data, read by examples/setup.sas: subjects of the CDISC pilot study, from the R packages pharmaverseadam and pharmaversesdtm. long program The program a one-call table (%table_summary, %table_ae, %table_model ...) writes and runs: the population, the records, one call per block, %stack and %table, the calls a person would write by hand. show = yes writes it to the log, show= with a file path (without quotes) to that file; start from it to add or change a block. numbers file The CSV file %ard writes: every number of a table, written with the format BEST32. (at most 15 significant digits, the last one cut, not rounded), and its printed text. output folder The folder where tables, figures and numbers files go. %study sets it; a program calls it &spl_out.. pattern The printed form of a statistic, written with X for the digits: XX.X prints one decimal. See How a number is kept and printed. result The data set a statistics macro writes (out=): one row per number, in the result shape. result shape The variables every result has: the group variables (of by=, and of var= or within= for a category or a level), GROUPS, BLOCK, STAT, VALUE and TEXT. setup setup= of %layout: the name of a global macro variable that %layout fills with the call of %print for its display data set. The program prints with %print(&<setup>.), such as %print(&t_first_print.). twin The numeric variable that gives the order of a character variable: TRT01AN is the twin of TRT01A. Macros sort columns by the twin (order= of %columns, %table and the one-call tables), and the groups of a comparison (order= of %lsmeans, %cox ...). order= of %freq is not a twin: order = frequency ranks the rows by their subjects and writes the rank into the twin of the variable. See How the parameters are named.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
These pages explain why the library works the way it does. They do not show how to do a task: the how-to guides do that. They do not list parameters: the reference does that.

  • How a program reads: the order of the calls, and why a program reads like the table it makes.
  • The result shape: the one data set that every statistics macro writes.
  • How a number is kept and printed: the full value, the pattern, the text.
  • How the parameters are named: the parameter names that mean different things in different macros.
  • One macro, one procedure: the rules the macros follow, and what they leave out on purpose.
  • What the proof shows: how the macros are checked against pharmaverse, and the limits of that check.

docs.title: How the parameters are named
docs.text: Most parameter names mean the same in every macro: data= is the input data set, where= the records to use, out= the result. A few names mean different things in different macros. This page lists them, so that a call of a new macro does not surprise you. The reference page of each macro gives the exact text.

docs.title: order=
docs.text:
Macros What order= is Example %columns, %table, %table_summary, %table_ae, %table_visit, %table_shift, %table_model, %table_response, %table_tte the numeric twin of the column variable: the columns are in its order order = trt01an %lsmeans, %mmrm, %cox, %logistic, %risk, %rateratio, %ttest, %wilcoxon the numeric twin of by=: the order of the groups, and so which group comes first in a pair order = trt01pn %freq a keyword, not a variable: frequency ranks the rows of orderof= by their subjects, the most first order = frequency %flag_first, %pick, %relchange the sort keys of the records within a group, as in a BY statement order = descending adt

%freq writes the rank of order = frequency into the twin of the variable (AEDECODN for AEDECOD), and %print orders the rows by it. %table_ae has the same ranking under another name, sort = frequency. sort= of %aeplot orders the terms of a figure: difference, frequency or alphabetical.

docs.title: by=
docs.text: Macros What by= is the statistics macros (%describe, %freq, %km, ...) the groups. The first variable gives the columns of the table; in %describe and %freq the others give its rows or its pages. the macros that compare groups (%lsmeans, %cox, %ttest, ...) the groups of the model: one character variable (trt01p, not trt01pn) the one-call tables (%table_*) the groups of the columns: one character variable the figure macros (%kmplot, %meanplot, ...) the groups: one curve, line, box or colour per group the ADaM steps (%baseline, %flag_first, %locf, %relchange, %param_wide, ...) the groups of records, such as the subject and the parameter (by = usubjid paramcd) %print the left columns of the listing, printed first; a repeated value is shown once %worst the variables of a row (by = aebodsys aedecod); the worst records of a subject are kept in each row %pool the variable whose every group must have min= records

docs.title: keep=
docs.text:
keep= names other variables to keep in a result, for the names and the order of its rows. Where a group has more than one value of such a variable, the macros take different values:

Macro The value kept %describe the largest value in the group (the ID statement of PROC MEANS) %freq the value of the first record of the category %table_visit, %table_shift keep= of the %describe or %freq calls they make %tte the value on the record taken (the event or the censoring); the variables must be in events= and in censors=

Keep only variables with one value per group, such as param with paramcd or avisitn with avisit: then the rule does not matter.

docs.title: where= and event=
docs.text:
where= is always a condition in parentheses: where = (anl01fl = 'Y'). In most macros it selects the records to use. In %flag_first it selects the records that can be flagged, in %flag_if_any the records of from= that set the flag, and in %forestplot and %lineplot the rows of the result to draw.

event= has two forms:

Macros What event= is Example %tte a condition on the records of events=, without parentheses (they are allowed) event = trtemfl = 'Y' %logistic, %risk, %table_response, %interaction_logistic the value of the response that is the event, in quotes event = "Y"

docs.title: file=
docs.text:
Macros What file= is It writes %ard, %csv a name, without a path and without an extension &spl_out./ard/<file>.csv; %csv into listings or the folder of folder= %print, %table, %table_* a path without an extension <file>.rtf and <file>.lst; %table and %table_* also the numbers file in ard, named after the last part of the path the figure macros a path without an extension <file>.png and <file>.rtf %layout a path without an extension, for the call of %print it prepares nothing itself: it goes into the setup

In %ard the default of file= is the name of the program that %study set. In %table and %table_*, a call without file= prints nothing.

docs.title: total=
docs.text:
Macros What total = yes does %describe, %freq adds the group Total: all groups of the first by= variable together. A text in quotes gives it another name (total = "All subjects"). %columns, %table says that the results have the group Total: it becomes the last column, with the N of all subjects of n= %table_summary, %table_ae, %table_visit, %table_shift adds the column Total

Give total= to the statistics macros and to %columns (or %table) together, with the same name: %columns needs it to put the Total last, with the N of all subjects of n=.

docs.title: label=
docs.text: Macros What label= is Example the statistics macros the label of the block, a text in quotes: the heading of the rows of one call label = "Age (years)" %print, %layout, %table the labels of columns: pairs name="text", separated by blanks label = %STR(row=" ")

docs.title: out=, new= and the macros that change data=
docs.text:
Macros What they write the statistics macros, %stack, %columns, %layout, %tte, %worst, %param_wide, %relchange ... a new data set, named in out= the figure macros the numbers they draw, in out= when it is given %baseline, %flag_first, %flag_if_any, %pick, %pool, %summarize a new variable, named in new=, in data=: they change data= in place %locf new records in data=, in place, and data= sorted

Two names of out= are not data sets: out= of %study is the output folder, and out= of %import_xpt is the folder that gets the data sets.

A macro that changes data= in place changes the data set you give it. Copy the records into a data set of your own first (DATA vs; SET advs; WHERE paramcd = 'SYSBP'; RUN;), so that a later step still has the original. Give new= a name that data= does not have yet. Only two macros are made for a variable that is there: %pick replaces it, with a NOTE in the log, and %baseline with replace = yes drops it and makes it again (with replace = no it writes the values into the variable that is there).

docs.title: stats=
docs.text:
Macros What stats= is Example the statistics macros the statistics, in the order of the rows, each name with the pattern of its printed number stats = n mean="XX.XX" sd %table_summary, %table_visit, %table_ae, %table_shift, %table_model the same, passed to the %describe, %freq or model calls they make %summarize_groups one summary per variable of vars=: sum, mean, max or min, with no pattern stats = sum max

A name without a pattern takes its default pattern: see the table of default patterns. A name the macro does not compute gives an empty row and no message, as that page says. %summarize has one statistic, in stat=.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Explanation: The result shape, How a number is kept and printed.
  • Glossary: the terms of these pages, such as twin and block.

docs.title: A name of a macro and a name of a method
docs.text: %ancova is the Type III test of one numeric term, such as a dose response. The ANCOVA comparison of the treatment groups (LS means and their differences) is %lsmeans, and %table_model with method = ancova calls %lsmeans, not %ancova.

docs.title: One macro, one procedure
docs.text: The macros follow a small number of rules. The rules make a program easy to read for a person who knows SAS but has never seen the library, and easy to check for a reviewer or a regulator.

docs.title: A macro holds the procedure it runs
docs.text: %describe contains its PROC MEANS. %freq contains its PROC FREQ. %lsmeans contains its PROC MIXED. A person who opens the file of a macro finds the procedure in it, with the options it uses. There is no dispatcher that chooses a procedure from a text, no table of metadata, and no option that is parsed back out of a string.

docs.title: Data in, data out
docs.text:
A macro reads data sets and writes data sets. It keeps no state between calls: a result goes from one call to the next only as a data set that the program names. Two calls with the same parameters give the same result. Every result is a data set in WORK that a person can open, print and change.

One parameter is a deliberate exception. setup= of %layout names a global macro variable that keeps the call of %print for the display data set, so that %print(&t14_2_01_print.) prints it again after a change. The program chooses the name and the log shows its value; no other macro reads it.

docs.title: The groups come from the data
docs.text: by= names a variable. The columns are its values. The program never lists the treatment arms.

docs.title: One printer
docs.text: %print holds the only PROC REPORT of the library. Every table and listing goes through it, so every output has the same look: <file>.rtf (ODS RTF, the style journal) and <file>.lst (a monospace listing). A figure is one call of its figure macro, with one PROC SGPLOT or PROC SGPANEL in it.

docs.title: A clear message, then stop
docs.text:
Every macro checks its parameters before it does anything. A wrong call writes two lines and stops:

ERROR: [describe] var=AGEX is not a variable of adsl
ERROR: [describe]   fix: give var= a variable of data=.

The first line names the parameter and the fault. The second line says what to change. No procedure runs on wrong input, so the log never fills with the errors of a procedure.

docs.title: What the library leaves out on purpose
docs.text: Not in the library Instead A population parameter in the building blocks a DATA step in the program, visible to the reviewer A list of treatments the values of by= Sorting of the input the program sorts; a statistics macro keeps the order it is given (an ADaM step such as %locf sorts the data it changes, as its page says) "(Continued)" lines, page headers, splits of wide tables by hand the titles and footnotes of the program; PROC REPORT pages and splits PROC SQL, PROC EXPORT DATA steps and procedures that a SAS programmer reads at a glance

docs.title: The tables in one call
docs.text: %table_summary, %table_ae and the other one-call tables are the exception to the building blocks: one call makes a whole standard table. Most of them take the population as a parameter, because a standard table always has one: the tables of records (%table_ae, %table_visit, %table_shift, %table_response, %table_model, %table_tte) have pop=, a condition on the subjects of adsl=; %table_summary reads one row per subject and selects them with where=; %table prints a table that the program stacked, so the program selects its population. They hide nothing: each call runs the long program it stands for, the same calls of %describe, %freq, %stack, %layout and %print that a programmer would write. show=yes writes that long program to the log, and show=<file> writes it to a file and runs it from there. A reviewer reads the long program; a programmer who needs a change starts from it.

docs.title: The house style
docs.text: Each macro file has the same parts in the same order: a header box (purpose, procedure, proof, parameters, output, example, change log), the signature with one parameter per line, the checks, numbered steps, and the deletion of its work data sets (kept with debug=yes). Keywords are upper case, names are lower case. A checker enforces these rules on every file.

docs.title: How a number is kept and printed
docs.text: Every number exists twice in a result: as VALUE, with every digit SAS computed, and as TEXT, the way the table prints it. The two never mix. A table shows TEXT; every check reads VALUE.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
stats= gives each statistic a pattern. The pattern shows the printed form of one number with a group of X:

Pattern The number Prints as Used for XX 75.2093 75 counts, minimum, maximum XX.X 75.2093 75.2 mean, median, LS mean, a difference XX.XX 75.2093 75.21 standard deviation, standard error (XX.X%) 75.2093 (75.2%) a percent (XX.X%) 9.46 ( 9.5%) a percent below 10 X.XXX 0.2451 0.245 a p-value

The number of X after the point is the number of decimals. The X before the point do not limit the number: XX prints 254 as 254. The text around the X group, such as the brackets and the percent sign, prints as written.

The number is right aligned in the width of the X group, and the text is then trimmed at both ends. So a pattern that starts with its X group never has a leading blank (9.46 with XX.X prints as 9.5), but a pattern with text before the group keeps the blank inside it: 9.46 with (XX.X%) prints as ( 9.5%), so that the brackets of a column line up. A number wider than the group is not cut: it pushes the text after it to the right.

docs.title: The table of default patterns
docs.text:
Each statistic has a default pattern, so stats= is needed only to change one. A name without a pattern in stats= takes the default pattern of its name: stats = n mean sd prints n with XX, the mean with XX.X and the SD with XX.XX. The defaults are the same in every macro:

Statistic names Default pattern n, events, min, max XX pct (XX.X%) pval X.XXX mean, median, q1, q3, lsmean, diff, estimate, lcl, ucl XX.X every other name: sd, se, diff_se, lsmean_se, lsmean_lcl, lsmean_ucl, hr, or, rr, rd, irr, rate, exposure, surv, ... XX.XX

Three defaults surprise at first. surv, the percent alive of %km, takes XX.XX: give surv="XX.X" for one decimal. rd, the risk difference, takes XX.XX as a name in stats=, but the default stats= of %risk gives it X.XXX. The limits of an LS mean (lsmean_lcl, lsmean_ucl) take XX.XX, the limits of a difference (lcl, ucl) XX.X. The default stats= of a macro (its reference page shows it) can give a pattern of its own, which wins over this table.

A name the macro does not compute gives an empty row, and no message

stats= is not checked against the statistics of the macro. A name the macro does not compute, such as a misspelt meen, gives a row with that STAT, a missing VALUE and a blank TEXT, and the log has no ERROR, no WARNING and no NOTE about it. The table then has a line with a label and no number. Use the names that the reference page of the macro lists under stats=, and look at the result before you print it.

%describe(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = age
   , by    = trt01a
   , stats = n="XX" mean="XX.XX" sd="XX.XX" median="XX.X" min="XX" max="XX"
   , out   = age
 )

The order of stats= is also the order of the lines in the table.

Minimum and maximum print as whole numbers by default

The default pattern of min and max is XX, which suits ages and counts. A laboratory value with decimals loses them: a minimum of 3.9 prints as 4. Give the pattern with the decimals of the data: stats = n mean sd median min="XX.X" max="XX.X".

docs.title: Rounding
docs.text: The text is ROUND(value, 10 ** -decimals): SAS rounds a tie away from zero, so 2.25 with XX.X prints as 2.3. R rounds a tie to the even digit and prints 2.2. Both are correct roundings of the same value. This is why the proof counts a reference number as the same when it is a correct rounding of the SAS value, either way.

docs.title: A p-value is never 0 or 1
docs.text: A p-value that rounds to 0 prints as <0.001 (with the pattern X.XXX), and one that rounds to 1 prints as >0.999. Only TEXT changes. VALUE keeps the number: a p-value of 0.00004 stays 0.00004 in the result and in the numbers file.

docs.title: The numbers file
docs.text:
%ard writes every VALUE of a table, and the N of each column, to a CSV file in the folder ard of the output folder. Its parameter file= is a name, not a path: file=t_first writes &spl_out./ard/t_first.csv. These are the first lines of the numbers file of the tutorial:

ard/t_first.csv: the first 7 of 45 lines
result,stat,g1_value,g2_value,g3_value,g4_value,g5_value,raw,formatted
N,n,Placebo,,,,,86,(N=86)
N,n,Xanomeline Low Dose,,,,,96,(N=96)
N,n,Xanomeline High Dose,,,,,72,(N=72)
N,n,Total,,,,,254,(N=254)
T_AGE,n,Placebo,,,,,86,86
T_AGE,mean,Placebo,,,,,75.2093023255814,75.2

Each line is one number: the result it comes from (result), its statistic (stat), its groups (g1_value to g5_value: the first is the column of the table, the others the levels of the row, at most five), the value written with the format BEST32. (raw) and the printed text (formatted). A second program, in SAS or in R, can compare its own numbers with this file without reading the table. The proof compares this file with the published numbers of pharmaverse.

raw is not the full value that SAS keeps. SAS keeps a number in 8 bytes, about 16 significant digits; BEST32. writes at most 15 significant digits and at most 14 decimals, and it cuts the digits after them: it does not round the last one. So 664/9 (73.77777777777777...) is written 73.7777777777777, not 73.7777777777778, and 2/3 is written 0.66666666666666. A whole number is written in full. A check that reads raw therefore compares with a small relative tolerance, such as METHOD=RELATIVE CRITERION=1E-10 of PROC COMPARE, never with exact equality.

docs.title: How a program reads
docs.text: A program that uses the library reads like the table it makes. A reviewer who reads the program from top to bottom sees the population, each block of the table, the columns, and the print. Nothing happens out of sight.

docs.title: The order of the calls
docs.text:
Every table program has the same five parts, in the same order, after the library is loaded (part 0).

%LET spl_root  = /opt/sapling-sas;                         /* 0. load the library  */
%LET studydir  = /studies/cdiscpilot01;
%INCLUDE "&spl_root./macros/sapling.sas";

%study(
     CDISCPILOT01
   , program = t14_2_01
   , adam    = &studydir./adam
   , out     = &studydir./out
 )                                                          /* 1. start the program */

DATA saf;                                                  /* 2. the population    */
  SET adam.adsl;
  WHERE saffl = 'Y';
RUN;

%describe(data=saf, var=age, by=trt01p, label="Age", out=t_age)     /* 3. one call per block */
%freq(data=saf, var=race, by=trt01p, label="Race", out=t_race)

%stack(t_age t_race, out=t14_2_01)                        /* 4. the table as data */
%columns(data=t14_2_01, n=saf, var=trt01p, order=trt01pn, out=t14_2_01_cols)
%ard(data=t14_2_01, columns=t14_2_01_cols, file=t14_2_01)
%layout(
     data    = t14_2_01
   , columns = t14_2_01_cols
   , var     = trt01p
   , file    = &spl_out./tlf/t14_2_01
   , setup   = t14_2_01_print
   , out     = t14_2_01_display
 )

TITLE1 "Table 14-2.01 Summary of Demographic and Baseline Characteristics";
%print(&t14_2_01_print.)                                  /* 5. the output        */
  1. Load the library. spl_root names the folder that holds macros/, and the loader macros/sapling.sas includes every macro. A program of a study does this once, at the top; a program run in a session that has the library already leaves it out. Use the macros in your own program shows the steps.
  2. Start. %study sets the options of the program, the library ADAM and the output folder &spl_out..
  3. The population. A plain DATA step selects the subjects. The macros do not hide a population inside a parameter.
  4. The blocks. Each block of the table is one call of one statistics macro: %describe for a number, %freq for categories, %ancova or %lsmeans for a model. Each call writes one data set, its result.
  5. The table as data. %stack puts the results under each other in the order of the table. %columns makes the columns and the N of each. %ard writes every number to a CSV file. %layout makes the display data set: one row per printed line, one variable per column.
  6. The output. The program writes its own titles and footnotes. %print prints the display data set as RTF and as a text listing.

A figure follows the same pattern up to part 3. Then one call of its figure macro (%kmplot, %meanplot, ...) computes what it draws and writes the figure.

docs.title: Why the steps are separate
docs.text:
Each step writes a data set that a person can open. A programmer who checks a table can stop after any step and look:

After Look at To check a statistics macro its result the numbers of one block %stack the stacked results the order of the blocks %columns the columns data set the column order and each N %ard the numbers file every number written with BEST32. (15 significant digits) and as printed %layout the display data set each printed line, before it is printed

A change in one step is made in one place. For example, a sponsor who wants another row label changes the display data set in a DATA step and prints it again with %print(&t14_2_01_print.). No statistic is computed again.

docs.title: The groups come from the data
docs.text: The columns of a table are the values of the by= variable. The program never types the treatment names. A study with four arms gives four columns without a change of the program. order= names the numeric variable that sorts the columns (trt01pn), and total=yes adds a column of all subjects.

docs.title: What the proof shows
docs.text: The library is checked against tables that other people made, in R, with the pharmaverse, and published. The check compares numbers, one by one. This page explains what the check shows and what it does not.

docs.title: The references
docs.text:
Reference What it is Outputs R Consortium R Submission Pilot 1 The CDISC pilot study made in R and reviewed by the FDA in 2022 demographics, the ADAS-Cog ANCOVA, the glucose ANCOVA, the Kaplan-Meier figure pharmaverse examples The tables that {rtables} and {tern} make from the test data of pharmaverseadam the demographic table, the adverse event table

Each reference is read at a fixed commit of its repository. The data are the data the reference used: the ADaM transport files of the pilot, and ADSL and ADAE of pharmaverseadam 1.3.0.

docs.title: How a number is compared
docs.text:
For each output, a SAS program calls the macros and writes the numbers file with %ard. A tool reads every number that the reference prints, from its text, its RTF or its PDF, and records where it read it. Then it compares:

  • A number is the same when the reference is the SAS value rounded to the decimals the reference prints. Either rounding of a tie counts, because SAS and R round a tie in different ways.
  • A number is explained when the reference computes it in another way, and the tool proves the explanation: it computes the number the way of the reference, from the SAS numbers, and gets the number of the reference. Example: the reference gives a confidence interval as estimate ± 1.96 × SE; SAS uses the t quantile; the SAS estimate and SE with 1.96 give the limits of the reference.
  • A number is not made when no macro computes it. It is declared with its reason and listed. It never counts as the same.

The tool also counts the numbers it reads from each reference and compares the count with the known count. A parser that loses a row makes the proof fail.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
Reference Numbers Same Explained Not made R Submission Pilot 1 231 228 2 1 pharmaverse examples 1,965 1,953 12 0

Every number, with the place in the reference it was read from and its verdict, is in the results folder of each suite of the repository. The results page of each suite lists its outputs and their counts: R Submission Pilot 1 and pharmaverse examples.

docs.title: What the proof does not show
docs.text:
• Only the outputs that were compared. The proof covers the statistics that these six outputs use: descriptive statistics, frequencies, ANCOVA with LS means, Kaplan-Meier, the adverse event counts. Each macro has its own check against known answers, but a macro that no reference uses is not part of this comparison.
  • Only the numbers, not the look. The layout of a SAS table differs from the layout of the reference. The proof compares numbers, not rows, fonts or page breaks.
  • Agreement, not truth. Two programs that agree can both be wrong in the same way. The references are independent of the library (other people, another language, other procedures), and one of them was reviewed by the FDA. That makes a shared error unlikely, not impossible.

docs.title: The result shape
docs.text: Every statistics macro writes its numbers in one shape, its result. %describe, %freq, %ancova, %km and the others all write the same variables. That is why %stack, %columns, %ard and %layout work with any of them, and why a programmer can read any result without the manual of its macro.

docs.title: One row per number
docs.text:
A result has one row per number. A row says which group the number belongs to, which statistic it is, and its value.

Variable Holds Example the by= variables the group, with the names and values of the data TRT01A = 'Placebo' the var= and within= variables the category or the level of the row: a category of %freq, a term of %fisher SEX = 'F' VERSUS the group a comparison is made against (only a macro that compares groups) 'Placebo' GROUPS the names of the group variables, in order 'TRT01A VERSUS' BLOCK the label of the block in the table (label=) 'Age (years)' STAT the statistic n, mean, sd, pct, diff, pval VALUE the number, with every digit 75.2093023255814 TEXT the number as the table prints it 75.2

This is the result of a call of %describe on the example data, its first rows:

%describe(data=adsl, var=age, by=trt01a, label="Age (years)", out=age)

age: the first 4 of 18 rows
TRT01A   GROUPS  BLOCK        STAT           VALUE  TEXT
Placebo  TRT01A  Age (years)  n                 86    86
Placebo  TRT01A  Age (years)  mean    75.209302326  75.2
Placebo  TRT01A  Age (years)  sd      8.5901671271  8.59
Placebo  TRT01A  Age (years)  median            76  76.0

The listing shows VALUE in at most 12 characters; the data set keeps the full value that SAS computed.

docs.title: Why one shape
docs.text:
A table mixes many kinds of numbers: counts, means, p-values, hazard ratios. If each macro wrote its own shape, each next step would need a branch for each macro. With one shape, the next steps read every result in the same way:

  • %stack puts results of different macros under each other.
  • %layout finds the line and the column of each number from BLOCK, STAT and the group variables.
  • %ard writes every VALUE to a CSV file, for a check against another program or another language.

The shape is long, not wide: one row per number, not one variable per statistic. A long shape keeps every number with its own label. A new statistic is a new value of STAT, not a new variable.

docs.title: No data qualified
docs.text:
When a statistics macro finds no record to use, it writes its result with no row and this line in the log:

NOTE: [describe] No data qualified: no record meets where= and the conditions of the macro.

It does not stop the program. When the whole table has no row, %print prints the text of nodata= (No data qualified by default) under the titles of the table. An empty table is a result of the study, not an error of the program.

docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
Each guide solves one task of a clinical SAS programmer, step by step. Each runs on the example data, so its output is shown under its code. The guides assume that you know SAS and the ADaM data. To learn the library from the start, do the tutorial first.

Guide The task it solves Use the macros in your own program Load the library from its own folder, read the ADaM transport files into the folder of the study, start a program with %study, and find the outputs. Derive analysis visits, the baseline and the change from baseline Add avisit, ablfl, anl01fl, base and chg to the records of a BDS data set. Make a demographic table with tests Summarize the characteristics of the subjects by treatment, with a p-value for each. Make an adverse event table Count the subjects with an event by system organ class and preferred term, with Fisher's exact test. Make an efficacy table with an ANCOVA Show an endpoint at a visit with the descriptive statistics, the LS means and their differences from an ANCOVA. Make a Kaplan-Meier figure with the number at risk Draw the curves of a time to an event by treatment, with the median and the log-rank p-value. Make one page per subgroup Print a table once for each value of a subgroup, with the N of each page. Check a table against an independent program Compare every number of a table with the numbers of a second program. Run the examples of the reference Run the examples of the reference pages in one session, in their order, and get the output the pages show.

docs.title: Make an adverse event table
docs.text: This guide shows how to make a table of the subjects with treatment-emergent adverse events, by system organ class and preferred term, with Fisher's exact test of each term. You get an RTF file, a text listing and a numbers file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Have two data sets: the population, one row per subject (adsl), and the adverse events, one row per event (adae). Both need the treatment variable of the columns (trt01a).
  • Know the condition of the events to count. The guide counts the treatment-emergent events: trtemfl = 'Y'.

docs.title: 1. Count the subjects with any event
docs.text:
Call %freq without var=. Give the population to denom=: each percent is then a percent of all subjects of the population, with or without an event.

%freq(
     data  = adae
   , denom = adsl
   , where = (trtemfl = 'Y')
   , by    = trt01a
   , label = "Subjects with at least one treatment-emergent adverse event"
   , out   = t_any
 )

t_any: 6 rows
TRT01A                STAT         VALUE  TEXT
Placebo               n               65  65
Placebo               pct   75.581395349  (75.6%)
Xanomeline High Dose  n               68  68
Xanomeline High Dose  pct   94.444444444  (94.4%)
Xanomeline Low Dose   n               84  84
Xanomeline Low Dose   pct           87.5  (87.5%)

docs.title: 2. Count the subjects in each system organ class
docs.text:
Call %freq with the class alone in var=. Each row counts the subjects with at least one event in the class:

%freq(
     data  = adae
   , denom = adsl
   , where = (trtemfl = 'Y')
   , var   = aebodsys
   , by    = trt01a
   , order = frequency
   , label = "System organ class"
   , out   = t_soc
 )

t_soc: the first 3 of 138 rows
TRT01A   AEBODSYS                                    STAT  TEXT
Placebo  CARDIAC DISORDERS                           n     12
Placebo  CARDIAC DISORDERS                           pct   (14.0%)
Placebo  CONGENITAL, FAMILIAL AND GENETIC DISORDERS  n     0

docs.title: 3. Count the subjects in each preferred term
docs.text:
Name the class and the term in var=, in their order of nesting. Add order = frequency to put the most frequent term first in each class:

%freq(
     data  = adae
   , denom = adsl
   , where = (trtemfl = 'Y')
   , var   = aebodsys aedecod
   , by    = trt01a
   , order = frequency
   , label = "Treatment-emergent adverse events"
   , out   = t_term
 )

A subject with two events of the same term counts once in its row. In this block the class is a heading over its terms: the heading has no count. The counts of the classes are the rows of the block of step 2.

docs.title: 4. Test each term
docs.text:
Call %fisher with the same records, the same denom= and the same label= as the counts. within= gives one test per term:

%fisher(
     data   = adae
   , denom  = adsl
   , where  = (trtemfl = 'Y')
   , by     = trt01a
   , within = aebodsys aedecod
   , label  = "Treatment-emergent adverse events"
   , out    = t_term_test
 )

t_term_test: the first 3 of 230 rows
AEBODSYS           AEDECOD              STAT   TEXT
CARDIAC DISORDERS  ATRIAL FIBRILLATION  pval  0.858
CARDIAC DISORDERS  ATRIAL FLUTTER       pval  0.743
CARDIAC DISORDERS  ATRIAL HYPERTROPHY   pval  0.622

Skip this step if the table has no p-values.

docs.title: 5. Stack the blocks and print the table
docs.text:
%table makes the columns, the numbers file, the display data set and the printed table in one call:

%stack(t_any t_soc t_term t_term_test, out=t_ae)
TITLE1 "Table 14.3.1 Treatment-emergent adverse events by system organ class and preferred term";
TITLE2 "Safety population";
FOOTNOTE1 J=L "A subject is counted once in each row. p-value: Fisher's exact test.";
%table(
     data  = t_ae
   , n     = adsl
   , var   = trt01a
   , order = trt01an
   , file  = &spl_out./tlf/t_ae
 )

docs.title: Check a table against an independent program
docs.text: This guide shows how to check every number of a table against the numbers of a second program, as in double programming. You compare the numbers file of the table with the numbers of the check program in PROC COMPARE, and get a report that lists each difference.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Have the program of the table. It must write the numbers file with %ard (or %table with file=). The guide checks a table of age and sex as in the tutorial.

docs.title: 1. Run the program of the table
docs.text:
This is the program the guide checks. %ard writes its numbers file, ard/t_dm.csv in the output folder:

%describe(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = age
   , by    = trt01a
   , total = yes
   , label = "Age (years)"
   , out   = t_age
 )
%freq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = sex
   , by    = trt01a
   , total = yes
   , label = "Sex"
   , out   = t_sex
 )
%stack(t_age t_sex, out=t_dm)
%columns(
     data  = t_dm
   , n     = adsl
   , var   = trt01a
   , order = trt01an
   , total = yes
   , out   = t_dm_cols
 )
%ard(data=t_dm, columns=t_dm_cols, file=t_dm)

ard/t_dm.csv: the first 6 of 45 lines
result,stat,g1_value,g2_value,g3_value,g4_value,g5_value,raw,formatted
N,n,Placebo,,,,,86,(N=86)
N,n,Xanomeline Low Dose,,,,,96,(N=96)
N,n,Xanomeline High Dose,,,,,72,(N=72)
N,n,Total,,,,,254,(N=254)
T_AGE,n,Placebo,,,,,86,86

docs.title: 2. Read the numbers file
docs.text:
Each line of the numbers file holds one number: its result, its statistic, the values of its groups, the number written with the format BEST32. (raw: at most 15 significant digits, the last one cut, not rounded; see How a number is kept and printed), and its printed text (formatted). Read it with a DATA step:

DATA prod;
  INFILE "&spl_out./ard/t_dm.csv" DSD FIRSTOBS=2 TRUNCOVER;
  LENGTH result stat $32 g1_value g2_value g3_value g4_value g5_value formatted $200;
  INPUT result stat g1_value g2_value g3_value g4_value g5_value raw formatted;
RUN;

prod: the first 8 of 44 rows
RESULT  STAT    G1_VALUE              G2_VALUE           RAW  FORMATTED
N       n       Placebo                                   86  (N=86)
N       n       Xanomeline Low Dose                       96  (N=96)
N       n       Xanomeline High Dose                      72  (N=72)
N       n       Total                                    254  (N=254)
T_AGE   n       Placebo                                   86  86
T_AGE   mean    Placebo                         75.209302326  75.2
T_AGE   sd      Placebo                         8.5901671271  8.59
T_AGE   median  Placebo                                   76  76.0

The first lines (result N) hold the N of each column. The other lines hold the numbers of the results, named as the results of the table program (T_AGE, T_SEX).

docs.title: 3. Compute the same numbers in the check program
docs.text:
Compute each number again with SAS procedures, without the macros. Write it in the same form: one row per number, with the same result, stat and group values. Add the group Total as a copy of every subject. %study sets VALIDVARNAME=UPCASE, so VNAME gives the name of a statistic in upper case: LOWCASE makes it the stat of the numbers file.

DATA qc_adsl;
  SET adsl;
  OUTPUT;
  trt01a = 'Total';
  OUTPUT;
RUN;

PROC FREQ DATA=qc_adsl NOPRINT;
  TABLES trt01a / OUT=qc_n;
  TABLES trt01a * sex / OUTPCT OUT=qc_sex;
RUN;

PROC MEANS DATA=qc_adsl NOPRINT NWAY;
  CLASS trt01a;
  VAR age;
  OUTPUT OUT=qc_age N=n MEAN=mean STD=sd MEDIAN=median MIN=min MAX=max;
RUN;

DATA qc;
  LENGTH result stat $32 g1_value g2_value $200;
  SET qc_n(IN=in_n) qc_age(IN=in_age) qc_sex(IN=in_sex);
  ARRAY s {*} n mean sd median min max;
  g1_value = trt01a;
  IF in_n THEN DO;
    result = 'N';
    stat   = 'n';
    raw    = count;
    OUTPUT;
  END;
  ELSE IF in_age THEN DO;
    result = 'T_AGE';
    DO i = 1 TO DIM(s);
      stat = LOWCASE(VNAME(s{i}));
      raw  = s{i};
      OUTPUT;
    END;
  END;
  ELSE IF in_sex THEN DO;
    result   = 'T_SEX';
    g2_value = sex;
    stat     = 'n';
    raw      = count;
    OUTPUT;
    stat = 'pct';
    raw  = pct_row;
    OUTPUT;
  END;
  KEEP result stat g1_value g2_value raw;
RUN;

docs.title: 4. Compare the two
docs.text:
Sort both by the keys of a number. Then compare raw in PROC COMPARE, and write the report to a file:

PROC SORT DATA=prod;
  BY result stat g1_value g2_value;
RUN;
PROC SORT DATA=qc;
  BY result stat g1_value g2_value;
RUN;

OPTIONS DLCREATEDIR;
LIBNAME checks "&spl_out./qc";
ODS LISTING FILE="&spl_out./qc/t_dm_compare.lst";
PROC COMPARE BASE=prod COMPARE=qc OUT=checks.t_dm_diff OUTNOEQUAL METHOD=RELATIVE CRITERION=1E-10;
  ID result stat g1_value g2_value;
  VAR raw;
RUN;
%LET compare_code = &sysinfo.;
ODS LISTING CLOSE;
ODS LISTING;

The report says that the two data sets have all 44 numbers in common and that no value differs by more than the criterion. 14 values are not exactly equal: the numbers file holds at most 15 significant digits, with the last one cut, and METHOD=RELATIVE CRITERION=1E-10 accepts a difference in the last digits.

docs.title: 5. Decide from the return code
docs.text:
An empty OUT= data set is not enough: it holds only the numbers that are in both data sets, so a number that one program has and the other does not never reaches it. Decide from the return code of PROC COMPARE, which step 4 kept in &compare_code.. Four of its bits matter: 64 (a number only in the numbers file), 128 (a number only in the check program), 4096 (a value outside the criterion) and 32768 (the comparison could not be done):

DATA verdict;
  LENGTH verdict $80;
  compare_code = &compare_code.;
  IF BAND(compare_code, 64 + 128 + 4096 + 32768) = 0 THEN
    verdict = 'checked: the same numbers on both sides, every value within the criterion';
  ELSE verdict = 'not checked: read the report of PROC COMPARE';
RUN;

verdict: 1 row
VERDICT                                                                    COMPARE_CODE
checked: the same numbers on both sides, every value within the criterion             0

If the verdict is "not checked", the report lists the numbers in one data set only and the values that differ. Find each number by its result, stat and group values, and look at the program that computed it.

This compares the values (raw). It does not check the printed text: a wrong pattern, such as one decimal where the shell asks for two, prints the right value wrongly. To check the text too, write your own text of each value with PUTN and the pattern of the shell, and compare it with formatted.

docs.title: Make a demographic table with tests
docs.text: This guide shows how to make a table of the demographic characteristics by treatment, with a p-value for each characteristic. You get an RTF file, a text listing and a numbers file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Make a data set of your population, one row per subject. The guide uses adsl, the safety population of the example data.
  • Decide which test each characteristic gets. The guide uses the analysis of variance for age, the chi-square test for the age group and sex, and Fisher's exact test for race.

docs.title: 1. Summarize each continuous characteristic
docs.text:
Call %describe for the statistics and %anova for the p-value. Give both the same label=: the p-value then prints in the block of the statistics, without a heading of its own.

%describe(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = age
   , by    = trt01a
   , total = yes
   , label = "Age (years)"
   , out   = t_age
 )
%anova(data=adsl, var=age, by=trt01a, label="Age (years)", out=t_age_test)

t_age_test: 1 row
BLOCK        STAT         VALUE   TEXT
Age (years)  pval  0.2346471181  0.235

The test compares the treatment groups only: total = yes of %describe adds the group Total to the statistics, not to the test.

docs.title: 2. Count each categorical characteristic
docs.text:
Call %freq for the counts and %chisq for the p-value:

%freq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = agegr1
   , by    = trt01a
   , total = yes
   , label = "Age group (years)"
   , out   = t_agegr
 )
%chisq(data=adsl, var=agegr1, by=trt01a, label="Age group (years)", out=t_agegr_test)
%freq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = sex
   , by    = trt01a
   , total = yes
   , label = "Sex"
   , out   = t_sex
 )
%chisq(data=adsl, var=sex, by=trt01a, label="Sex", out=t_sex_test)

If a characteristic has categories with few subjects, as race has here, use Fisher's exact test: add exact = yes to %chisq.

%freq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = race
   , by    = trt01a
   , total = yes
   , label = "Race"
   , out   = t_race
 )
%chisq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = race
   , by    = trt01a
   , exact = yes
   , label = "Race"
   , out   = t_race_test
 )

docs.title: 3. Stack the blocks in the order of the table
docs.text:
Name each result, and its test after it:

%stack(
     results = t_age t_age_test t_agegr t_agegr_test t_sex t_sex_test t_race t_race_test
   , out     = t_demog
 )

docs.title: 4. Make the columns and the numbers file
docs.text:
Take the N of each column from the population, and order the columns by the numeric twin of the treatment:

%columns(
     data  = t_demog
   , n     = adsl
   , var   = trt01a
   , order = trt01an
   , total = yes
   , out   = t_demog_cols
 )
%ard(data=t_demog, columns=t_demog_cols, file=t_demog)

docs.title: 5. Lay out and print the table
docs.text:
Give format= the format that decodes a category. Then write the titles and the footnotes, and print:

%layout(
     data    = t_demog
   , columns = t_demog_cols
   , var     = trt01a
   , format  = sex $sexf.
   , file    = &spl_out./tlf/t_demog
   , setup   = t_demog_print
   , out     = t_demog_display
 )
TITLE1 "Table 14.1.1 Demographic characteristics";
TITLE2 "Safety population";
FOOTNOTE1 J=L "p-values: age, analysis of variance; age group and sex, chi-square test;";
FOOTNOTE2 J=L "race, Fisher's exact test.";
%print(&t_demog_print.)

docs.title: Derive analysis visits, the baseline and the change from baseline
docs.text: This guide shows how to derive the analysis variables of a BDS data set such as ADVS from its collected records: the analysis visit of each record by its study day, the baseline flag, one analysis record per visit, the baseline value and the change from baseline.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Have the records with the value (aval) and the study day (ady), one row per measurement. The guide starts from the blood pressure records of advs and keeps only the collected variables.
  • Have the visit windows and the baseline rule of the plan. The guide uses: baseline is the last value on or before day 1; Week 4, Week 12 and Week 24 are windows around their target days.
DATA vs;
  SET advs;
  WHERE paramcd IN ('SYSBP' 'DIABP');
  KEEP usubjid trt01a paramcd param adt ady aval vsseq;
RUN;

vs: the first 5 of 5851 rows
USUBJID      TRT01A   ADT      ADY  PARAM                            PARAMCD  AVAL  VSSEQ
01-701-1015  Placebo  26DEC13   -7  Diastolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)  DIABP      64      1
01-701-1015  Placebo  31DEC13   -2  Diastolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)  DIABP      68      4
01-701-1015  Placebo  02JAN14    1  Diastolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)  DIABP      56      7
01-701-1015  Placebo  14JAN14   13  Diastolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)  DIABP      67     10
01-701-1015  Placebo  16JAN14   15  Diastolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)  DIABP      56     13

docs.title: 1. Put each record in its analysis window
docs.text:
Call %windows with one window per analysis visit, # between the windows. A window is its number (avisitn), its name, its first day, its last day, its target day and its range as printed. A period is a limit that is open:

%windows(
     data    = vs
   , windows = 0  "Baseline" .   1   1   "<=1"
             # 4  "Week 4"   2   42  28  "2-42"
             # 12 "Week 12"  43  126 84  "43-126"
             # 24 "Week 24"  127 210 168 "127-210"
   , day     = ady
 )

%windows changes vs in place. It adds avisit, avisitn, the limits of the window and awtdiff, the distance of the record from the target day. A record in no window keeps them missing.

docs.title: 2. Flag the baseline record
docs.text:
Call %flag_first on the records that can be the baseline, and choose the last one by the study day:

%flag_first(
     data  = vs
   , where = (ady <= 1 AND NOT MISSING(aval))
   , by    = usubjid paramcd
   , order = ady vsseq
   , which = last
   , new   = ablfl
 )

docs.title: 3. Flag one analysis record per visit
docs.text:
Call %flag_first again, by visit. The record nearest to the target day is chosen first. On a tie, the earlier day wins, then the earlier record:

%flag_first(
     data  = vs
   , where = (NOT MISSING(avisitn) AND NOT MISSING(aval))
   , by    = usubjid paramcd avisitn
   , order = awtdiff ady vsseq
   , new   = anl01fl
 )

docs.title: 4. Give every record its baseline value
docs.text:
Call %baseline. It copies aval of the record with ablfl = 'Y' to every record of the subject and parameter:

%baseline(data=vs, value=aval, by=usubjid paramcd, new=base)

docs.title: 5. Compute the change from baseline
docs.text:
Compute the change in a DATA step, after the baseline visit only:

DATA vs;
  SET vs;
  IF avisitn > 0 AND NOT MISSING(base) THEN chg = aval - base;
RUN;

vs where usubjid = '01-701-1015' AND paramcd = 'SYSBP': 15 rows
USUBJID      PARAMCD  ADY  AVISIT    AWTDIFF  AVAL  ABLFL  ANL01FL  BASE  CHG
01-701-1015  SYSBP     -7  Baseline        8   131                   130
01-701-1015  SYSBP     -2  Baseline        3   138                   130
01-701-1015  SYSBP      1  Baseline        0   130  Y      Y         130
01-701-1015  SYSBP     13  Week 4         15   137                   130    7
01-701-1015  SYSBP     15  Week 4         13   114                   130  -16
01-701-1015  SYSBP     29  Week 4          1   138         Y         130    8
01-701-1015  SYSBP     31  Week 4          3   138                   130    8
01-701-1015  SYSBP     42  Week 4         14   148                   130   18
01-701-1015  SYSBP     63  Week 12        21   138                   130    8
01-701-1015  SYSBP     84  Week 12         0   139         Y         130    9
01-701-1015  SYSBP     84  Week 12         0   139                   130    9
01-701-1015  SYSBP    126  Week 12        42   163                   130   33

docs.title: Make an efficacy table with an ANCOVA
docs.text: This guide shows how to make a table of a continuous endpoint at one visit: the descriptive statistics of the baseline, the value and the change from baseline, then the LS means and their differences from an analysis of covariance. You get an RTF file, a text listing and a numbers file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Have the analysis records: one record per subject at the visit, with the baseline (base), the value (aval) and the change (chg). The guide uses the systolic blood pressure of advs at Week 12.
  • Know the model of the plan: the response, the covariates, the class factors and the pairs of groups to compare. The guide models the change with the baseline as covariate and compares each dose with placebo.
  • Know the analysis population of the plan. An efficacy table is usually on the efficacy or full analysis population, by the planned treatment (TRT01P). The example data have no flag of such a population (no EFFFL, no ITTFL): the guide uses the safety population (SAFFL) of examples/setup.sas, by the planned treatment. With your own data, select the population of the plan in step 1 and give its subjects to n=.

docs.title: 1. Select the analysis records
docs.text:
Select the parameter, the visit and the analysis flag in a DATA step:

DATA sbp;
  SET advs;
  WHERE paramcd = 'SYSBP' AND avisit = 'Week 12' AND anl01fl = 'Y';
RUN;

sbp: the first 3 of 150 rows
USUBJID      TRT01P                AVISIT   BASE  AVAL  CHG
01-701-1015  Placebo               Week 12   130   139    9
01-701-1028  Xanomeline High Dose  Week 12   138   128  -10
01-701-1034  Xanomeline High Dose  Week 12   163   145  -18

The analysis flag anl01fl selects one record per subject at each visit. The model needs exactly one.

docs.title: 2. Describe the baseline, the value and the change
docs.text:
Call %describe once for each variable, each with its own label:

%describe(data=sbp, var=base, by=trt01p, label="Baseline (mmHg)", out=t_base)
%describe(data=sbp, var=aval, by=trt01p, label="Week 12 (mmHg)", out=t_aval)
%describe(data=sbp, var=chg, by=trt01p, label="Change from baseline (mmHg)", out=t_chg)

docs.title: 3. Fit the ANCOVA
docs.text:
Call %lsmeans with the change as var= and the baseline as covariate. Name each pair of groups, the group first and then the group it is compared with. Ask for the LS means in stats=:

%lsmeans(
     data   = sbp
   , var    = chg
   , by     = trt01p
   , covars = base
   , pairs  = "Xanomeline Low Dose" "Placebo"
            # "Xanomeline High Dose" "Placebo"
   , order  = trt01pn
   , stats  = lsmean="XX.X" lsmean_se="XX.XX" diff="XX.X" diff_se="XX.XX" lcl="XX.X" ucl="XX.X"
              pval="X.XXX"
   , label  = "ANCOVA of the change from baseline"
   , out    = t_model
 )

t_model: the first 8 of 16 rows
TRT01P                VERSUS   STAT       TEXT
Placebo                        lsmean     -3.2
Placebo                        lsmean_se  1.58
Xanomeline High Dose           lsmean     -8.9
Xanomeline High Dose           lsmean_se  2.03
Xanomeline Low Dose            lsmean     -3.1
Xanomeline Low Dose            lsmean_se  2.03
Xanomeline High Dose  Placebo  diff       -5.7
Xanomeline High Dose  Placebo  diff_se    2.57

The rows with a blank VERSUS hold the LS mean of each group. The other rows compare a group with the group in VERSUS. To add a class factor, such as a site or a stratum, give it in class=.

docs.title: 4. Test the dose response
docs.text:
If the plan also tests a trend over the doses, call %ancova with the numeric dose in test=:

%ancova(
     data   = sbp
   , var    = chg
   , covars = base
   , test   = trt01pn
   , label  = "Test of the dose response"
   , out    = t_dose
 )

Skip this step if the plan has no such test.

docs.title: 5. Stack the blocks and print the table
docs.text:
%stack(t_base t_aval t_chg t_model t_dose, out=t_eff)
TITLE1 "Table 14.4.1 Systolic blood pressure (mmHg): ANCOVA of the change from baseline at Week 12";
TITLE2 "Safety population, by planned treatment";
FOOTNOTE1 J=L "ANCOVA: change from baseline = baseline + treatment.";
FOOTNOTE2 J=L "Difference: the dose group minus placebo, with its 95% confidence interval.";
%table(
     data  = t_eff
   , n     = adsl
   , var   = trt01p
   , order = trt01pn
   , file  = &spl_out./tlf/t_eff
 )

docs.title: Make the table in one call
docs.text:
%table_model makes the descriptive blocks and the ANCOVA block of this table from the records of all visits. Give the visit of the table in at=, the population in adsl= (the N of the columns) and the labels of the blocks in names=. Its table differs from the table above in two things:

  • It has no test of the dose response, and so no column All groups. Add it with the long program (show = yes) and the %ancova call of step 4.
  • The ANCOVA block has the label the macro gives it, ANCOVA, adjusted for base.

Like %print, it prints the TITLE and FOOTNOTE statements in force: set them before the call.

TITLE1 "Table 14.4.2 Systolic blood pressure (mmHg): ANCOVA of the change from baseline at Week 12";
%table_model(
     data     = advs
   , adsl     = adsl
   , where    = (paramcd = 'SYSBP' AND anl01fl = 'Y')
   , covars   = base
   , by       = trt01p
   , at       = "Week 12"
   , order    = trt01pn
   , describe = base aval chg
   , pairs    = "Xanomeline Low Dose" "Placebo"
              # "Xanomeline High Dose" "Placebo"
   , names    = base="Baseline (mmHg)" aval="Week 12 (mmHg)" chg="Change from baseline (mmHg)"
   , file     = &spl_out./tlf/t_eff_short
 )

docs.title: Make a Kaplan-Meier figure with the number at risk
docs.text: This guide shows how to draw the Kaplan-Meier curves of a time to an event by treatment, with the number at risk under the axis, the median of each group, and the log-rank p-value in a footnote. You get a PNG file and an RTF file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Have one record per subject with the time (aval) and the censoring variable (cnsr, 1 = censored). If your data have no such parameter yet, step 1 derives it.
  • Have the population, one row per subject (adsl), for the order of the curves.

docs.title: 1. Derive the time to the event
docs.text:
Skip this step if your ADTTE has the parameter. The guide derives the time to the first treatment-emergent skin event, from the first dose. A subject without an event is censored at the date of the last dose (censor_date = trtedt). The call has no end=, so an event after the last dose still counts; give end = trtedt to count only the events up to the end of treatment:

%tte(
     subjects      = adsl
   , events        = adae
   , event         = trtemfl = 'Y' AND aebodsys = 'SKIN AND SUBCUTANEOUS TISSUE DISORDERS'
   , date          = astdt
   , start         = trtsdt
   , censor_date   = trtedt
   , seq           = aeseq
   , censor_desc   = "End of treatment"
   , censor_source = "ADSL"
   , event_desc    = aedecod
   , source        = "ADAE"
   , paramcd       = "TTSKIN"
   , out           = ttskin
 )

ttskin: the first 4 of 252 rows
USUBJID      TRT01A                PARAMCD  ADT        CNSR  AVAL  EVNTDESC
01-701-1015  Placebo               TTSKIN   02JUL2014     1   182  End of treatment
01-701-1023  Placebo               TTSKIN   07AUG2012     0     3  ERYTHEMA
01-701-1028  Xanomeline High Dose  TTSKIN   14JAN2014     1   180  End of treatment
01-701-1033  Xanomeline Low Dose   TTSKIN   31MAR2014     1    14  End of treatment

A subject with no event and no date of the last dose (trtedt missing) has neither an event nor a censoring, so %tte writes no record for it. Find such subjects before you draw. The example data have two:

PROC SORT DATA=ttskin OUT=tte_ids(KEEP=usubjid) NODUPKEY; BY usubjid; RUN;
PROC SORT DATA=adsl OUT=adsl_ids(KEEP=usubjid trt01a trtsdt trtedt); BY usubjid; RUN;
DATA no_record;
  MERGE adsl_ids tte_ids(IN=in_tte);
  BY usubjid;
  IF NOT in_tte;
RUN;

no_record: 2 rows
USUBJID      TRT01A               TRTSDT   TRTEDT
01-705-1018  Placebo              05JUL13
01-705-1382  Xanomeline Low Dose  13MAY13

These two subjects are in the N of their columns, which comes from adsl, but not in the curves: at day 0 the Placebo curve has 85 subjects at risk of N=86, and the Xanomeline Low Dose curve 95 of N=96.

docs.title: 2. Summarize the curves and make the columns
docs.text:
Call %km for the median of each group and its confidence interval:

%km(data=ttskin, var=aval, by=trt01a, label="Time to the first skin event (days)", out=t_km)

t_km where stat NE 'n' AND stat NE 'events': 9 rows
TRT01A                STAT    VALUE  TEXT
Placebo               median         NE
Placebo               lcl            NE
Placebo               ucl            NE
Xanomeline High Dose  median     57  57.0
Xanomeline High Dose  lcl        46  46.0
Xanomeline High Dose  ucl       177  177.0
Xanomeline Low Dose   median     80  80.0
Xanomeline Low Dose   lcl        51  51.0
Xanomeline Low Dose   ucl            NE

NE is a median or a limit that the curve does not reach: the Placebo curve stays above 50%. Then call %columns on the result of %km: the columns give the order of the curves and their colors.

%columns(data=t_km, n=adsl, var=trt01a, order=trt01an, out=t_km_cols)

COL  COLVALUE              BIGN
  1  Placebo                 86
  2  Xanomeline Low Dose     96
  3  Xanomeline High Dose    72

docs.title: 3. Put the log-rank p-value into a footnote
docs.text:
Call %logrank, then keep the printed text of its p-value in a macro variable:

%logrank(data=ttskin, var=aval, by=trt01a, out=t_logrank)
DATA _NULL_;
  SET t_logrank;
  CALL SYMPUTX('pval', text);
RUN;

t_logrank: 1 row
STAT        VALUE  TEXT
pval  3.216126E-6  <0.001

docs.title: 4. Draw the figure
docs.text:
Write the titles and the footnotes, then call %kmplot. median = yes writes the median of each group and its confidence interval in the plot. xlabel= and ylabel= name the axes:

TITLE1 "Figure 14.2.1 Time to the first skin event";
TITLE2 "Safety population";
FOOTNOTE1 J=L "p-value of the log-rank test: &pval.";
%kmplot(
     data    = ttskin
   , columns = t_km_cols
   , time    = aval
   , by      = trt01a
   , median  = yes
   , xlabel  = "Days from the first dose"
   , ylabel  = "Subjects without a skin event (%)"
   , file    = &spl_out./figures/f_ttskin
   , out     = f_ttskin
 )

The number at risk under the axis counts the subjects whose time is the time of the tick or later. To choose the ticks, give their times in times=, such as times = 0 30 60 90 120 150 180.

PROC PRINT DATA=f_ttskin NOOBS;

  VAR trt01a x n;
RUN;

docs.title: Use the macros in your own program
docs.text: This guide shows how to start a program of your own study with the library: load the macros from the folder of the library, read the ADaM transport files into the folder of the study, start the program with %study, and find the outputs. The tutorial and the other guides start from examples/setup.sas, which does the same for the example data.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Have a copy of the repository datastep-labs/sapling-sas, or of its folder macros, in a folder that SAS can read: the folder of the library, such as /opt/sapling-sas.
  • Have the folder of the study, such as /studies/cdiscpilot01, with the ADaM data in its folder adam, as SAS data sets or as transport files (.xpt).
  • Know the folder where the program may write its tables, figures and numbers files, such as the folder out of the study.

The library and the study are two folders. One copy of the library serves every study; a study holds its data and its outputs, never the macros.

docs.title: 1. Load the library
docs.text:
Set spl_root to the folder of the library, the folder that holds macros/, then include the loader macros/sapling.sas. It includes every macro of the library, so that each one is ready to call:

%LET spl_root = /opt/sapling-sas;  /* the folder of the library: it holds macros/ */
%INCLUDE "&spl_root./macros/sapling.sas";

spl_root is a global macro variable that the library reads: the loader includes each macro as &spl_root./macros/<name>.sas, so spl_root must be the folder of the library, not the folder of the study. Write the path without quotes and without a slash at the end. Load the library once per SAS session: a second %INCLUDE compiles the macros again and changes nothing.

Name the folder of the study in a macro variable of your own, for the steps below. On the example data, the folder of the study is the folder examples of the library:

%LET studydir = &spl_root./examples;  /* the folder of the study: data/, adam/ and out/ */

docs.title: 2. Read the ADaM transport files
docs.text:
Skip this step if your ADaM data are SAS data sets already. %import_xpt copies each transport file into a SAS data set of a folder. members= names the data sets; the macro reads <dir>/<member>.xpt (or the same name in lower case). Read the ADaM data sets that the program uses into the folder adam of the study. The folder of out= must exist; OPTIONS DLCREATEDIR; lets the LIBNAME statement of the macro make it:

OPTIONS DLCREATEDIR;
%import_xpt(
     dir     = &studydir./data
   , members = adsl adae
   , out     = &studydir./adam
 )

The library reads ADaM data sets: the statistics macros and the tables need the variables of ADaM, such as TRT01A, SAFFL and AVAL. Make the ADaM data sets from the SDTM data before this program, in the programs of the ADaM.

%import_xpt stands alone: a program that only converts the data may include macros/import_xpt.sas without the rest of the library.

docs.title: 3. Start the program with %study
docs.text:
Call %study once, at the top of each program, before any other macro of the library. Its first value is the name of the study, without a keyword and without quotes. program= is the name of this program:

%study(
     CDISCPILOT01
   , program = t14_1_01
   , adam    = &studydir./adam
   , out     = &studydir./out
 )

sashelp.vmacro where name = 'SPL_STUDY' OR name = 'SPL_PROGRAM': 2 rows
NAME         VALUE
SPL_PROGRAM  t14_1_01
SPL_STUDY    CDISCPILOT01

%study does four things:

  • It sets the global macro variables SPL_STUDY (the study), SPL_PROGRAM (the program, in lower case) and SPL_OUT (the output folder). %ard names its numbers file after SPL_PROGRAM when its file= is not given.
  • It opens the folder of adam= as the library ADAM, read only.
  • It sets the output folder, out=. The programs write their files under it as &spl_out./....
  • It sets the options of the outputs (NODATE NONUMBER NOCENTER, MISSING=' ' and the others of its reference page) and clears the TITLE and FOOTNOTE statements.

The defaults of adam= and out= are &spl_root./adam and &spl_root./out: folders of the library. With the library in a folder of its own, always give adam= and out=, the folders of the study.

A macro reads the data set of its data=, never the library ADAM by itself. Select the population in a DATA step of the program:

DATA saf;
  SET adam.adsl;
  WHERE saffl = 'Y';
RUN;

saf: the first 5 of 254 rows
USUBJID      TRT01A                SAFFL
01-701-1015  Placebo               Y
01-701-1023  Placebo               Y
01-701-1028  Xanomeline High Dose  Y
01-701-1033  Xanomeline Low Dose   Y
01-701-1034  Xanomeline High Dose  Y

docs.title: 4. Write the outputs into their folders
docs.text:
Each output goes into one folder of the output folder. A program gives the path in file=:

Folder What goes there Written by &spl_out./tlf the tables, as <file>.rtf and <file>.lst %print, the one-call tables (%table, %table_summary, ...) &spl_out./listings the listings, and the CSV files of %csv %print, %csv &spl_out./figures the figures, as <file>.png and <file>.rtf, and the numbers of a figure as CSV the figure macros (%kmplot, %meanplot, ...), %csv with folder = figures &spl_out./ard the numbers files, one CSV file per output %ard

A folder that is missing is made when a macro writes its first file there, with a NOTE in the log that names it. For example, a table of age by treatment goes to &spl_out./tlf/t14_1_01, and its numbers to &spl_out./ard:

%describe(data=saf, var=age, by=trt01a, label="Age (years)", out=t_age)
%stack(t_age, out=t_age_table)
%columns(data=t_age_table, n=saf, var=trt01a, order=trt01an, out=t_age_cols)
%ard(data=t_age_table, columns=t_age_cols)

ard/t14_1_01.csv: the first 6 of 22 lines
result,stat,g1_value,g2_value,g3_value,g4_value,g5_value,raw,formatted
N,n,Placebo,,,,,86,(N=86)
N,n,Xanomeline Low Dose,,,,,96,(N=96)
N,n,Xanomeline High Dose,,,,,72,(N=72)
T_AGE,n,Placebo,,,,,86,86
T_AGE,mean,Placebo,,,,,75.2093023255814,75.2

docs.title: 5. Keep the log short
docs.text:
Every macro writes a line to the log when it begins and when it ends (NOTE: [describe] begins ...). To leave these lines out, set the global macro variable spl_quiet before the calls:

%LET spl_quiet = yes;

The messages of a wrong call (ERROR and WARNING) are still written. Set %LET spl_quiet = no; to have the lines again.

docs.title: The whole start of a program
docs.text:
%LET spl_root = /opt/sapling-sas;         /* the folder of the library */
%LET studydir = /studies/cdiscpilot01;    /* the folder of the study */
%INCLUDE "&spl_root./macros/sapling.sas";
%LET spl_quiet = yes;

%study(
     CDISCPILOT01
   , program = t14_1_01
   , adam    = &studydir./adam
   , out     = &studydir./out
 )

DATA saf;
  SET adam.adsl;
  WHERE saffl = 'Y';
RUN;

The macros come from /opt/sapling-sas/macros, the ADaM data sets from /studies/cdiscpilot01/adam, and the outputs go to /studies/cdiscpilot01/out. Another study needs only another studydir.

docs.title: Make one page per subgroup
docs.text: This guide shows how to print a table once for each value of a subgroup variable, such as sex, with the N of each column counted on its page and the value in the title. All pages go into one RTF file and one text listing.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Submit examples/setup.sas, or start your own program as Use the macros in your own program shows.
  • Have the population, one row per subject, with the subgroup variable. The guide uses adsl and makes one page per sex.
  • Have a format for the values of the subgroup if the title should print a label, such as $sexf. of the example data (F = Female).

docs.title: 1. Compute each block by treatment and subgroup
docs.text:
Give the subgroup as the second variable of by= in every statistics macro:

%describe(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = age
   , by    = trt01a sex
   , total = yes
   , label = "Age (years)"
   , out   = t_age
 )
%freq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = agegr1
   , by    = trt01a sex
   , total = yes
   , label = "Age group (years)"
   , out   = t_agegr
 )
%freq(
     data  = adsl
   , var   = race
   , by    = trt01a sex
   , total = yes
   , label = "Race"
   , out   = t_race
 )
%stack(t_age t_agegr t_race, out=t_sub)

docs.title: 2. Make the columns of each page
docs.text:
Give the subgroup to page= of %columns. The N of a column is then the N of its page:

%columns(
     data  = t_sub
   , n     = adsl
   , var   = trt01a
   , order = trt01an
   , page  = sex
   , total = yes
   , out   = t_sub_cols
 )

t_sub_cols: 8 rows
SEX  COL  HEADER                       BIGN

F      2  Xanomeline Low Dose|(N=55)     55
F      3  Xanomeline High Dose|(N=35)    35

M      2  Xanomeline Low Dose|(N=41)     41
M      3  Xanomeline High Dose|(N=37)    37
M      4  Total|(N=111)                 111

docs.title: 3. Lay out the pages
docs.text:
Give the same page= to %layout, and the format of the subgroup to format=:

%layout(
     data    = t_sub
   , columns = t_sub_cols
   , var     = trt01a
   , page    = sex
   , format  = sex $sexf.
   , file    = &spl_out./tlf/t_sub
   , setup   = t_sub_print
   , out     = t_sub_display
 )

docs.title: 4. Name the subgroup in the title and print
docs.text:
%print prints each page under a BY statement. Set OPTIONS NOBYLINE and put #BYVAL1 in a title: the title then names the value of the page. Set OPTIONS BYLINE again after the print:

OPTIONS NOBYLINE;
TITLE1 "Table 14.1.3 Demographic characteristics by sex";
TITLE2 "Sex: #BYVAL1";
TITLE3 "Safety population";
%print(&t_sub_print.)
OPTIONS BYLINE;

docs.title: Run the examples of the reference
docs.text: This guide shows how to run the examples of the reference pages yourself, with the same output as the pages show. Each reference page has examples, and under each call the output that call made when the examples ran on SAS.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Have a copy of the repository datastep-labs/sapling-sas and SAS 9.4.
  • Set the path in examples/setup.sas, as the tutorial shows.

docs.title: Why one session and one order
docs.text:
The examples ran in one SAS session, after examples/setup.sas, one macro after the other. A later example may read a data set that an earlier example made with its out=: the example of %columns reads the table that the example of %stack made, and the example of %kmplot reads the time to an event of %tte. Each reference page says which data sets its examples read from another example, under "They also read", with a link to that example.

So run the examples in the same session and in the order below. An example that you run alone, out of this order, may stop with an ERROR because a data set it reads does not exist yet.

docs.title: 1. Run the setup
docs.text: Submit the whole of examples/setup.sas. It loads the macros, reads the example data, calls %study, and makes the WORK data sets adsl (the safety population), adae, advs, adlb, adtte and adrs that the examples read.

docs.title: 2. Run the examples in this order
docs.text: The program examples/reference.sas holds every example in this order: submit it after examples/setup.sas, in the same session, whole or one part after another. To run the examples of one page by hand, submit the pages before it first, in the order below: the parts in their order, and in each part the pages in the order of its list. The code of a page is all its blocks, top to bottom.

docs.title: Read the data and start the program
docs.text:
%tte comes this early because its result, adttde, is the time to an event that %km, %logrank, %cox, %kmplot and %table_tte read.

  1. %import_xpt
  2. %study
  3. %tte

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
Each statistics macro writes a result. %adjust reads the result of %lsmeans.

  1. %describe
  2. %anova
  3. %freq
  4. %chisq
  5. %worst
  6. %termflags
  7. %fisher
  8. %cmh
  9. %proportion
  10. %risk
  11. %logistic
  12. %rate
  13. %rateratio
  14. %ancova
  15. %lsmeans
  16. %adjust
  17. %mmrm
  18. %ttest
  19. %wilcoxon
  20. %interaction_glm
  21. %interaction_logistic
  22. %interaction_genmod
  23. %km
  24. %logrank
  25. %cox
  26. %interaction_phreg

docs.title: Build a table
docs.text:
%stack stacks the results of %describe, %anova, %freq and %chisq; %columns, %ard, %layout and %print then work on that table, each on what the call before it made.

  1. %stack
  2. %columns
  3. %ard
  4. %layout
  5. %print
  6. %table
  7. %csv

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
The figures take their order and their colors from the columns of %columns. %lineplot draws the numbers that %meanplot kept.

  1. %kmplot
  2. %forestplot
  3. %meanplot
  4. %lineplot
  5. %boxplot
  6. %barplot

  8. %profileplot
  9. %scatterplot
